title: Suspected Hepatobiliary Malignancy - RUQ Pain with Nodular Hepatomegaly
patient_instructions: You are Denise Carmody, a 55-year-old woman with a dull ache under the right ribs (right upper tummy) for about 3 months. It is a constant nagging discomfort, not colicky. You have lost about 6 kg without trying and your appetite has fallen away. You feel tired. You travelled to rural Queensland a couple of months ago for a caravan holiday. If asked about alcohol, you drink about 6 full-strength beers every day and have done so for years. Your father had 'cancer of the bile duct'. No fevers or shakes, no yellowing that you have noticed, no itch, no vomiting blood, no black stools. No chest pain or shortness of breath. You take no regular medications; no allergies. Your IDEAS: you think it might be your 'liver playing up' from the beers. Your CONCERNS: you are frightened it could be serious because of your father. Your EXPECTATIONS: you want to know what is going on and what tests are needed. Affect: guarded about the drinking, becomes tearful if the word cancer is used - the doctor should use a warning shot and be gentle. If the candidate asks the examiner for examination findings, they will be told the liver is enlarged, non-tender and nodular.
candidate_instructions: Setting: General practice / medical clinic. Denise Carmody, 55, presents with 3 months of right upper quadrant pain. Tasks: (1) Take a focused history (approximately 3-4 minutes). (2) Ask the examiner for the relevant physical examination findings. (3) Explain your most likely diagnosis and differentials to the patient and outline initial investigation. The examiner is looking for elicitation of constitutional red flags and risk factors, correct interpretation of a nodular non-tender liver, and a sensitive explanation that raises the possibility of cancer without giving an unconfirmed definitive diagnosis.
examiner_instructions: If asked, give: liver enlarged, firm, NON-TENDER and NODULAR; no obvious jaundice. The candidate should elicit RUQ pain for 3 months, weight loss, anorexia, heavy alcohol use (about 6 beers/day, roughly 8+ standard drinks, well above the guideline of no more than 10 standard drinks/week), family history of biliary (bile duct) cancer, and recent Queensland travel. Expected reasoning: chronic heavy alcohol causes cirrhosis, and cirrhosis is the dominant risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma; a nodular non-tender liver with constitutional red flags suggests HCC in a cirrhotic liver, with cholangiocarcinoma/gallbladder cancer also possible. Keep cholangiocarcinoma (bile ducts) and gallbladder carcinoma as distinct entities. Differentials: hepatitis (viral/alcoholic), cholangitis, cholecystitis, pancreatitis/pancreatic cancer, plus upper-abdominal mimics ACS and lower-lobe pneumonia. Expected plan: LFTs, FBE, coagulation, hepatitis B/C serology, AFP, triple-phase CT/MRI liver, urgent hepatobiliary referral; do not biopsy before specialist imaging review. Reward a SPIKES-style warning shot ('I am concerned this could be a cancer and we need urgent tests') rather than a definitive diagnosis. Use the rubric.

criteria: Elicits constitutional red flags (weight loss, anorexia, fatigue)
Quantifies alcohol in standard drinks and takes family history
Requests and correctly notes nodular non-tender hepatomegaly
States malignancy (HCC / biliary tract cancer) as top diagnosis with the alcohol-cirrhosis-HCC reasoning
Keeps cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder cancer distinct; gives coherent differentials including upper-abdominal mimics
Orders LFTs, FBE, coagulation, hepatitis B/C serology, AFP and triple-phase CT/MRI liver
Urgent hepatobiliary referral (Optimal Care Pathway); does not biopsy before specialist imaging; brief alcohol intervention/withdrawal awareness
Warning shot and plain-language explanation avoiding an unconfirmed definitive cancer diagnosis; explores ICE

red_flags: Unintentional weight loss and loss of appetite over 3 months (constitutional red flags)
Nodular, firm, non-tender hepatomegaly (suggests malignancy/cirrhosis rather than infection)
Chronic heavy alcohol use (about 8+ standard drinks/day) - cirrhosis and HCC risk
Family history of biliary tract cancer with persistent RUQ pain
australian_guidelines: Australian alcohol guidelines (NHMRC): no more than 10 standard drinks per week; screen with AUDIT-C and provide brief intervention (RACGP SNAP framework); assess withdrawal risk if admitted

Optimal Care Pathway for hepatocellular carcinoma: LFTs, FBE, coagulation, hepatitis B/C serology, alpha-fetoprotein and triple-phase contrast CT or MRI liver, with urgent hepatobiliary referral; avoid biopsy before specialist imaging review
Medical Board of Australia Good Medical Practice / SPIKES: raise the possibility of cancer with a warning shot and check understanding rather than giving an unconfirmed definitive diagnosis
learning_objectives: Interpret nodular non-tender hepatomegaly in the context of constitutional red flags
Explain the alcohol-cirrhosis-hepatocellular carcinoma causal chain
Plan an evidence-based hepatobiliary malignancy work-up
key_points: A nodular non-tender liver in a heavy drinker with weight loss suggests HCC arising in a cirrhotic liver
Cholangiocarcinoma (bile ducts) and gallbladder carcinoma are distinct biliary tract cancers
Quantify alcohol in standard drinks; one 375 mL full-strength beer is about 1.4 standard drinks
Do not biopsy suspected HCC before specialist multiphase imaging review

citations.claim: Abdominal pain assessment in Australian general practice, including causes and clinical investigations, is covered in Murtagh's abdominal pain chapter, against which this RUQ pain differential approach is consistent.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.3476

citations.claim: Palpation of the liver edge for enlargement, tenderness and nodularity follows the systematic abdominal examination method of Talley & O'Connor, used to interpret the non-tender nodular hepatomegaly.
citations.source: Talley and O'Connor's Clinical Examination (8th edition).pdf, p.668

citations.claim: Constitutional red flags and referral thresholds in general practice support treating weight loss and anorexia as referral-triggering red flags.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.3549
